title: Security Review - Encryption / KMS / BYOK / HSM - Zephyr Payments
next_steps: Send SOC2 summary & KMS integration guide
Schedule follow-up deep-dive with Infra team (week of Jul 27)
action_items: Jordan: Email SOC2 report and link to security whitepaper - due 2026-07-17
Maya: Produce rough KMS/BYOK sequence diagram and circulate - due 2026-07-22

summary: Customer (Zephyr Payments) walked through encryption requirements for payments data. Main topics: encryption at rest/in transit, KMS integrations, BYOK and HSM support, audit logs, SSO/RBAC mapping. Redwood team explained hosted vs private options, BYOK flow, and audit log capabilities. Agreed to share SOC 2 docs and a BYOK/HSM architecture diagram; follow-up deep dive planned.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood, and with me is Maya Chen our solutions engineer. quick check, audio ok?
[00:06] Carlos Ramirez: Yep, good here. thanks Jordan.
[00:10] Aisha Khan: All good. we have about 50 minutes, we'll go high-level and then deep dive on the BYOK parts.
[00:18] Jordan Lee: Perfect, the agenda - quick security posture overview, walk through encryption at rest + in transit, KMS/BYOK/HSM options, audit logs, then Q&A and next steps.
[00:28] Maya Chen: I can kick off with how Redwood handles keys across our deployment modes - hosted, dedicated, private - and then we'll zoom into BYOK and HSM patterns.
[00:36] Devon Park: Great. to set context, we are a payments processor, so PCI scope matters, we need key control and strong rotation agreements, also data never leaves eu region for eu tenants.
[00:45] Jordan Lee: Totally understood. quick validation - you're considering both hosted API for speed and Redwood Private (VPC) for higher control, right?
[00:52] Carlos Ramirez: Exactly. we started with PineAI evals but their key management was limited; we want something that supports our KMS, BYOK, and optionally HSM-backed keys.
[01:02] Maya Chen: Understood. quick note: some transcript words might come out odd, but the core is - for hosted mode we offer envelope encryption with our cloud KMS by default, and we support BYOK where customers bring keys from their KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault).
[01:18] Aisha Khan: When you say BYOK, do you mean the raw model artifacts are encrypted with our key or just the data blobs? we need to ensure key material never lands on third-party systems unencrypted.
[01:27] Maya Chen: Good question. with BYOK our customers provide a CMK in their cloud KMS. Redwood encrypts the content encryption keys (CEKs) with that CMK - so the plaintext CEK is never persisted. we keep only wrapped keys. model weights are stored encrypted at rest; the wrapped CEKs are what we carry for decrypt on demand.
[01:42] Devon Park: And rotation? if we rotate keys in our KMS, how do you handle re-wrapping?
[01:48] Maya Chen: We support key rotation via a re-wrapping workflow: when you schedule rotation, Redwood will fetch the latest public key metadata and re-wrap CEKs with the new key version. we keep audit logs for the wrap/unwarp operations. note: for hosted customers we rely on cross-account IAM roles for key access.
[02:03] Carlos Ramirez: Cross-account iam - we need that flow documented. can you do cross-account with customer-managed HSM?
[02:08] Jordan Lee: Yes. for HSM-backed keys (Cloud HSM or external HSM delivered via partner) we support an HSM-backed CMK. the difference is the key material is non-exportable and all wrap/unwrap happens via the customer's KMS API. Redwood never has access to raw key material.
[02:23] Aisha Khan: Interesting, so Redwood calls our KMS to decrypt CEKs when needed? that implies a live network call, will that add latency to inference?
[02:30] Maya Chen: minimal impact. we cache the wrapped CEKs and only call KMS on initial unwrap or when cache expires. we use an envelope pattern: CEK unwrap happens once per model load or per instance bootstrap. overall token-level latency is unaffected after initial load.
[02:45] Devon Park: ok, that helps. one concern - for burst autoscale scenarios, if many instances start simultaneously, could that hit our KMS quotas?
[02:52] Maya Chen: good callout. we have guidance: configure a warm pool and stagger instance creation; Redwood also supports pre-unwrapping under a maintenance window, and we can coordinate with your KMS quota settings. we add exponential backoff and jitter for unwrap calls.
[03:06] Carlos Ramirez: For Private deployment - if we run the control plane in our VPC, does Redwood still need any key access?
[03:12] Jordan Lee: For Redwood Private with a customer-managed control plane, you can configure the KMS to be fully within your VPC and grant the control plane access via private endpoints. in that mode Redwood's hosted control plane has no access to key material - all wrap/unwrap calls occur within your network.
[03:26] Aisha Khan: And auditability - we need an immutable record of key operations, who triggered unwrap, timestamps, and the calling principal. how are your audit logs structured?
[03:34] Maya Chen: We produce detailed audit logs per request: operation type (unwrap/wrap/rotate), resource, request id, Redwood principal (service account id), and correlation ids. logs can be exported to your SIEM via syslog or pushed to your cloud storage with retention policies.
[03:46] Carlos Ramirez: retention - we need 7 years for some records. is that supported?
[03:50] Jordan Lee: Yes, for enterprise plans we support long-term archival to your storage; Redwood retains a short internal trace and you get the full export for your retention schedule.
[03:59] Devon Park: About encryption in transit - you use TLS 1.2+? mutual TLS?
[04:03] Maya Chen: We enforce TLS 1.2 minimum and prefer 1.3. for higher assurance we support mTLS between customer VPC and Redwood Dedicated endpoints. For Private you can enforce internal network controls and use service-to-service mTLS.
[04:16] Aisha Khan: For SSO and RBAC, can we map our Okta groups to Redwood roles and ensure least privilege for key unwrap operations?
[04:24] Jordan Lee: Yes, we support SAML SSO with SCIM provisioning; group-to-role mapping is configurable. unwrap operations are restricted to service principals - humans generally don't perform unwraps at runtime, but admin actions like rotate/unwrap-for-rewrap are gated by RBAC and audit.
[04:39] Carlos Ramirez: Do you do a separate encryption key per customer or per workspace?
[04:43] Maya Chen: Typically per-customer CMK is recommended. we can also support multiple keys per workspace if you want dataset-level separation.
[04:50] Devon Park: Are there compliance attestations for your hosted KMS usage?
[04:54] Jordan Lee: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II and we maintain other certifications; the hosted KMS flow uses our cloud provider's KMS which is itself compliant. we'll share the SOC2 summary and relevant control mappings.
[05:05] Aisha Khan: Please send the mapping to PCI control references as well - we handle cardholder data, want to see where Redwood reduces our scope.
[05:12] Jordan Lee: Noted, we'll include a PCI controls mapping doc.
[05:15] Maya Chen: small technical note - for inference state like KV cache, we also encrypt caches at rest and bind them to the CEK. ephemeral caches are cleared on instance termination.
[05:25] Carlos Ramirez: Good. how do you handle key compromise scenarios? say a CMK is suspected compromised - what's the playbook?
[05:31] Maya Chen: we have an incident playbook: immediate suspension of the CMK usage, re-wrap all CEKs with a new CMK, force redeploy/rebootstrap of instances, and produce an incident audit with all wrap/unwrap call logs. we can also support key revocation flows if your KMS supports them.
[05:46] Devon Park: That implies a coordinated maintenance window. we'll need SLA language around that for Dedicated/Private.
[05:51] Jordan Lee: Absolutely, that's part of the Dedicated/Enterprise contract - include response times and remediation windows.
[05:58] Aisha Khan: One more - HSM vendor compatibility. we run an on-prem Thales HSM and also use AWS CloudHSM in some regions. do you have patterns for both?
[06:08] Maya Chen: Yes, we've done integrations with both Thales and CloudHSM. pattern is the same: use the HSM-backed CMK, Redwood never sees key material; we call KMS endpoints or an on-prem connector. for on-prem HSMs we use a secure connector that tunnels control-plane calls over a customer-managed VPN.
[06:24] Carlos Ramirez: Are there any differences in latency for on-prem HSM?
[06:28] Maya Chen: slightly higher for on-prem HSM due to network hop, but again it's mostly during boot/unwrap. careful architecture (caching, warm pools) mitigates runtime impact.
[06:38] Devon Park: Ok let's talk audit logs again - can we push logs to our Splunk with a signed envelope? we require signed logs ingestion.
[06:45] Maya Chen: We can push logs to your S3/Blob and you can pick them up into Splunk. for signed envelopes we can add a HMAC signature per batch using a customer-provided signing key. we'll include details in the integration guide.
[06:58] Carlos Ramirez: What's the retention and what fields are included in each log line?
[07:02] Maya Chen: fields: timestamp, operation, resource id, request id, principal id, source ip, result code, correlation id. retention configurable per export; internal retention by default 90 days but exports can satisfy longer retention.
[07:16] Aisha Khan: Are there any known limitations with multi-region keys? we want eu keys for eu data residency and us keys for us. can Redwood route requests so keys never cross boundary?
[07:25] Jordan Lee: Yes. Redwood supports region scoping. you can provision per-region CMKs and configure routing policies so eu-region model instances only use eu keys. for hosted customers we maintain region isolation; for Private you run the control plane in-region for full locality.
[07:40] Devon Park: If we wanted to do zero-trust - no Redwood-hosted control plane access to keys ever - can we fully isolate keys?
[07:48] Maya Chen: For full isolation the on-prem/private deployment is the recommended path: control plane and KMS in your network, no external key calls. Redwood's operations then run via your private endpoints.
[07:58] Carlos Ramirez: Ok that's probably our target. what's the next step to validate feasibility?
[08:02] Jordan Lee: We'll share three things: SOC2 summary, KMS/BYOK integration guide with diagrams, and an HSM connector reference. then schedule a follow-up deep-dive with your infra team to walk through VPN, quota plans, and a short POC scope.
[08:15] Aisha Khan: Sounds good. please include an estimated timeline and any impacts to SLA for Private deployment.
[08:21] Jordan Lee: will do.
[08:24] Maya Chen: quick note - we sometimes see transcription swap Redwood product names; when I say 'CEK' that's content encryption key, 'CMK' customer master key; 'KV cache' is the inference cache.
[08:36] Carlos Ramirez: thanks Maya, that's helpful.
[08:40] Devon Park: couple quick clarifications - does Redwood require any long-term key escrow? we prefer no escrow.
[08:45] Jordan Lee: no escrow by default. for hosted customers if you opt-in to BYOK you retain key control; Redwood holds only wrapped CEKs. we can do escrow under specific contractual terms but it's not default.
[08:58] Aisha Khan: ok no escrow is preferred. also we need to validate your penetration test reports and third-party audit cadence.
[09:04] Jordan Lee: we'll include the pentest summary and an overview of our audit cadence.
[09:09] Maya Chen: quick operational question - what are your peak scale characteristics? that determines guidance on KMS quotas and warm pools.
[09:15] Carlos Ramirez: we do spikes up to 5k concurrent requests across 200 instances for a few minutes daily.
[09:23] Maya Chen: noted, we'll include warm pool guidance and quota planning.
[09:28] Jordan Lee: ok we're nearing the end, final recap?
[09:31] Aisha Khan: recap: share SOC2 + PCI mapping, BYOK/HSM architecture diagram, KMS integration guide, signed log envelope options, and schedule infra deep-dive. action items captured.
[09:41] Jordan Lee: Perfect. we'll send materials by Friday and get the deep-dive scheduled for week of Jul 27. thanks everyone.
[09:48] Carlos Ramirez: thanks.
[09:50] Aisha Khan: thanks, bye.
[09:52] Devon Park: bye.
